claim: Each k-fiber in HeLa cells in metaphase is composed of approximately nine KMTs.
source: Here, we show by large-scale electron tomography that each k-fiber in HeLa cells in metaphase is composed of approximately nine KMTs, only half of which reach the spindle pole.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and is supported by quantitative data from electron tomography reconstructions presented in the results section (Figure 3B shows 8.5 ± 2.2 KMTs per kinetochore, mean ±STD, n=292).

claim: Only half of the KMTs in HeLa metaphase spindles reach the spindle pole.
source: Here, we show by large-scale electron tomography that each k-fiber in HeLa cells in metaphase is composed of approximately nine KMTs, only half of which reach the spindle pole.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing that 49% (±15.5%, ±STD, n=3) of KMT minus ends were positioned within the defined MT-centrosome interaction area (Figure 5C).

claim: K-fibers exhibit remarkable variation in circumference and KMT density along their length.
source: We found that k-fibers exhibit remarkable variation in circumference and KMT density along their length, with the pole-proximal side showing a broadening.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative analysis of k-fiber cross-sections showing variation in polygonal area along the pole-to-kinetochore axis (Figure 7B).

claim: The pole-proximal side of k-fibers shows a broadening.
source: We found that k-fibers exhibit remarkable variation in circumference and KMT density along their length, with the pole-proximal side showing a broadening.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by measurements showing the average polygonal area of k-fibers was about threefold higher at the spindle poles compared to the kinetochores (Figure 7B).

claim: The association of KMTs with non-KMTs predominantly occurs in the spindle pole regions.
source: Extending our structural analysis then to other MTs in the spindle, we further observed that the association of KMTs with non-KMTs predominantly occurs in the spindle pole regions.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing that 60.7 ± 9.4% of KMT minus-end associations with MT lattices were observed at the spindle poles (Figure 8A).

claim: Mitotic spindles can contain thousands of MTs.
source: While mitotic spindles can contain thousands of MTs, only a fraction of those highly dynamic filaments is associated with the kinetochores (Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Redemann et al., 2017) and confirmed by the current study showing approximately 6300 MTs per spindle (6278 ± 1614 MTs, mean ±STD; Figure 2C–E; Table 1).

claim: Only a fraction of MTs in mitotic spindles is associated with the kinetochores.
source: While mitotic spindles can contain thousands of MTs, only a fraction of those highly dynamic filaments is associated with the kinetochores (Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and confirmed by data showing only ~14% of all MTs in the reconstructed spindles were KMTs (Table 1).

claim: KMTs are called kinetochore microtubules and function to establish a physical connection between the chromosomes and the rest of the spindle.
source: These MTs are called kinetochore microtubules (KMTs) and function to establish a physical connection between the chromosomes and the rest of the spindle (Flemming, 1879; Khodjakov et al., 1997; Maiato et al., 2004; Musacchio and Desai, 2017; Rieder, 1981; Rieder and Salmon, 1998).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: K-fibers in PtK1 cells are composed of about 20 KMTs.
source: Nevertheless, by applying serial thin-section TEM it was reported that k-fibers in PtK1 cells are composed of about 20 KMTs (McDonald et al., 1992; McEwen et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (McDonald et al., 1992; McEwen et al., 1997).

claim: Tomographic analysis of RPE1 cells revealed 12.6 ± 1.7 KMTs per k-fiber.
source: In contrast, tomographic analysis of RPE1 cells revealed 12.6 ± 1.7 KMTs per k-fiber (O'Toole et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study (O'Toole et al., 2020).

claim: Single KMTs are connected to the kinetochores in budding yeast.
source: Single KMTs are connected to the kinetochores in budding yeast (Winey et al., 1995), while multiple KMTs are connected to dispersed kinetochores in nematodes (Oegema et al., 2001; O'Toole et al., 2003; Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Winey et al., 1995).

claim: Multiple KMTs are connected to dispersed kinetochores in nematodes.
source: Single KMTs are connected to the kinetochores in budding yeast (Winey et al., 1995), while multiple KMTs are connected to dispersed kinetochores in nematodes (Oegema et al., 2001; O'Toole et al., 2003; Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Oegema et al., 2001; O'Toole et al., 2003; Redemann et al., 2017).

claim: Multiple KMTs connected to kinetochores are organized into bundles termed 'kinetochore-fibers' (k-fibers) in human cells.
source: Multiple KMTs connected to kinetochores are also observed in human cells. However, KMTs in these cells are organized into bundles, termed 'kinetochore-fibers' (k-fibers), which are attached to a single region on each chromosome (Begley et al., 2021; Godek et al., 2015; Inoue, 1953; Metzner, 1894; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984; O'Toole et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature (Begley et al., 2021; Godek et al., 2015; Inoue, 1953; Metzner, 1894; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984; O'Toole et al., 2020).

claim: The three reconstructed metaphase spindles were composed of approximately 6300 MTs (6278 ± 1614 MTs, mean ±STD).
source: Each of these metaphase spindles was composed of approximately 6300 MTs (6278 ± 1614 MTs, mean ±STD; Figure 2C–E; Table 1, Table 2) and had an average pole-to-pole distance of 9.0 ± 1.7 µm (mean ±STD; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by quantitative data from the 3D reconstructions shown in Figure 2 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The reconstructed metaphase spindles had an average pole-to-pole distance of 9.0 ± 1.7 µm (mean ±STD).
source: Each of these metaphase spindles was composed of approximately 6300 MTs (6278 ± 1614 MTs, mean ±STD; Figure 2C–E; Table 1, Table 2) and had an average pole-to-pole distance of 9.0 ± 1.7 µm (mean ±STD; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B and Table 1.

claim: Between 90 and 110 k-fibers per cell were identified in the tomographic data sets.
source: In our tomographic data sets, we identified between 90 and 110 k-fibers per cell, which included on average 859 ± 218 KMTs (mean ±STD, n=3; Figure 2F–H; Figure 2—videos 4–6; Table 1) in each spindle.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The k-fibers included on average 859 ± 218 KMTs (mean ±STD, n=3) in each spindle.
source: In our tomographic data sets, we identified between 90 and 110 k-fibers per cell, which included on average 859 ± 218 KMTs (mean ±STD, n=3; Figure 2F–H; Figure 2—videos 4–6; Table 1) in each spindle.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Only ~14% of all MTs in the reconstructed spindles were KMTs.
source: Thus, only ~14% of all MTs in the reconstructed spindles were KMTs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and can be calculated from the data in Table 1 showing the number of KMTs versus total MTs.

claim: The majority of annotated KMTs displayed open flared ends at the kinetochore.
source: The majority of annotated KMTs displayed open flared ends at the kinetochore (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), consistent with previous observations on the morphology of KMT plus ends in mammalian cells (McIntosh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by images in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and citation to previous work (McIntosh et al., 2013).

claim: The average distance between the sister k-fiber ends was 1.13 ± 0.24 µm (mean ±STD, n=292).
source: The average distance between the sister k-fiber ends was 1.13 ± 0.24 µm (mean ±STD, n=292).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C-D and Table 1.

claim: The number of KMT attachments to kinetochores in metaphase is not influenced by a variation in the inter-kinetochore distance.
source: We did not observe a correlation between these parameters (Figure 3C–D; Pearson's correlation coefficients were 0.04 and 0.29) and concluded that the number of KMT attachments to kinetochores in metaphase is not influenced by a variation in the inter-kinetochore distance.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C-D with Pearson's correlation coefficients of 0.04 and 0.29.

claim: The position of the k-fibers within the spindle has no effect on the average number of KMTs per k-fiber.
source: However, we did not find a difference in the number of attached KMTs for these three different regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3N; Table 5) and concluded that also the position of the k-fibers within the spindle has no effect on the average number of KMTs per k-fiber.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3N and Table 5.

claim: The measured average kinetochore area was 0.10 ± 0.07 µm2 (mean ±STD).
source: The measured average kinetochore area was 0.10 ± 0.07 µm2 (mean ±STD; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: The density of KMTs at the outer kinetochores was 112 ± 60 KMTs/µm2 (mean ±STD, n=292).
source: We then analyzed the density of KMTs at the outer kinetochores by counting the number of KMTs within the determined areas, which was 112 ± 60 KMTs/µm2 (mean ±STD, n=292; Figure 3—figure supplement 2D; Table 3).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and Table 3.

claim: The average center-to-center distance between neighboring KMTs was 74 ± 22 nm (mean ±STD, n=292).
source: In addition, we observed an average center-to-center distance between neighboring KMTs of 74 ± 22 nm (mean ±STD, n=292; Figure 3—figure supplement 2E; Table 4).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and Table 4.

claim: The average wall-to-wall spacing between KMTs at the outer kinetochore is about 50 nm.
source: Considering an MT diameter of 25 nm, this corresponds to an average wall-to-wall spacing of about 50 nm between the KMTs at the outer kinetochore.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and calculated from the center-to-center distance measurement (74 nm) minus the MT diameter (25 nm).

claim: KMTs had an average length of 3.87 ± 1.98 µm (mean ±STD, n=2579).
source: We also measured the length of the KMTs in our reconstructed k-fibers and observed a broad distribution of KMT lengths with an average value of 3.87 ± 1.98 µm (mean ±STD, n=2579; Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Table 3).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and Table 3.

claim: About 20 ± 4% of the KMTs had lengths less than 2 µm.
source: Indeed, about 20 ± 4% of the KMTs had lengths less than 2 µm.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and can be calculated from the length distribution data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: About 39 ± 10% of KMTs were longer than the half spindle length.
source: Our analysis also showed relatively long KMTs (about 39 ± 10%) that were longer than the half spindle length.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and can be calculated from the length distribution data.

claim: 49% (±15.5%, ±STD, n=3) of the KMT minus ends were positioned within the defined MT-centrosome interaction area.
source: Taking our determined cut-off value into account, we found that only 49% (±15.5%, ±STD, n=3) of the KMT minus ends were positioned within the defined MT-centrosome interaction area.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Table 3.

claim: The average number of KMTs per k-fiber at the spindle pole was 4.1 ± 2.0 (mean ±STD).
source: This is in accord with our observation that the average number of KMTs per k-fiber at the spindle pole (4.1 ± 2.0, mean ±STD; Figure 5—figure supplement 3; Table 3) was lower compared to the average number of KMTs per k-fiber at the kinetochore (8.5 ± 2.2, mean ±STD; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Table 3.

claim: Only half of the KMTs in HeLa cells are directly connected to the spindle pole, while the other half are indirectly connected.
source: All in all, this suggested to us that only half of the KMTs in HeLa cells are directly connected to the spindle pole, while the other half of the KMTs are indirectly connected.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and inferred from the data showing 49% of KMT minus ends within the MT-centrosome interaction area.

claim: Non-KMTs had an average length of 2.0 ± 1.7 µm (mean ±STD; n=14458).
source: Non-KMTs had an average length of 2.0 ± 1.7 µm (mean ±STD; n=14458; Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) showing a high number of very short (<2 µm) and a low number of long MTs (>half spindle length).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, and Table 3.

claim: 38 ± 9% of the non-KMT minus ends were localized in the defined MT-centrosome interaction zone.
source: In addition, 38 ± 9% of the non-KMT minus ends were localized in the defined MT-centrosome interaction zone and the remaining ~60% were located in the bulk of the spindle (Figure 5E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; Table 3).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5E and Table 3.

claim: The average value of KMT tortuosity was 1.1 ± 0.1 (mean ±STD, n=2579).
source: For all data sets, we observed an average value of KMT tortuosity of 1.1 ± 0.1 (mean ±STD, n=2579).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 6E and Table 4.

claim: 62 ± 8% of the KMTs showed a tortuosity of lower than 1.1.
source: We found that 62 ± 8% of the KMTs showed a tortuosity of lower than 1.1 and 38 ± 10% of the KMTs displayed a tortuosity higher than 1.1 (Figure 6E; Table 4).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 6E and Table 4.

claim: 38 ± 10% of the KMTs displayed a tortuosity higher than 1.1.
source: We found that 62 ± 8% of the KMTs showed a tortuosity of lower than 1.1 and 38 ± 10% of the KMTs displayed a tortuosity higher than 1.1 (Figure 6E; Table 4).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 6E and Table 4.

claim: Straight KMTs (tortuosity <1.1) were predominantly located in the center of the spindle, while curved KMTs (tortuosity >1.1) were located more at peripheral spindle positions.
source: We also observed that straight KMTs (tortuosity <1.1) were predominantly located in the center of the spindle, while curved KMTs (tortuosity >1.1) were located more at peripheral spindle positions (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Table 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and Table 5.

claim: The global tortuosity of KMTs was correlated with their length (R = 0.68; p = 2.2e-16).
source: Furthermore, the global tortuosity of KMTs was correlated with their length. As expected, short KMTs were straighter, while long KMTs were more curved (R = 0.68; p = 2.2e-16; Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6G with R = 0.68 and p = 2.2e-16.

claim: 75 ± 6% of the KMTs with a tortuosity higher than 1.1 were longer than the half-spindle length.
source: In addition, 75 ± 6% of the KMTs with a tortuosity higher than 1.1 were longer than the half-spindle length.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and can be calculated from the tortuosity and length distribution data.

claim: The local tortuosity of KMTs was weakly correlated with the relative position of the KMT segments on the pole-to-kinetochore axis (R = –0.13; p = 2.2e-16).
source: Importantly, the local tortuosity of the KMTs was weakly correlated with the relative position of the KMT segments on the pole-to-kinetochore axis. The local tortuosity slowly and constantly increased from the kinetochores towards the spindle poles (R = –0.13; p = 2.2e-16; Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6I with R = –0.13 and p = 2.2e-16.

claim: KMTs have a higher tortuosity at the spindle poles compared to the kinetochores.
source: Extending previously published knowledge, we concluded that KMTs have a higher tortuosity at the spindle poles compared to the kinetochores.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by the local tortuosity analysis shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Cross-sections of k-fibers showed an average polygonal area of 0.097 ± 0.161 µm2 (mean ±STD, n=292).
source: Cross-sections of k-fibers showed an average polygonal area of 0.097 ± 0.161 µm2 (mean ±STD, n=292).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 7B and Table 4.

claim: The average polygonal area of k-fibers was 0.034 ± 0.019 µm2 at the kinetochores.
source: We measured an average polygonal area of 0.034 ± 0.019 µm2 at the kinetochores, 0.149 ± 0.210 µm2 in the middle of the spindles, and 0.092 ± 0.146 µm2 at the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and can be calculated from the data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The average polygonal area of k-fibers was 0.149 ± 0.210 µm2 in the middle of the spindles.
source: We measured an average polygonal area of 0.034 ± 0.019 µm2 at the kinetochores, 0.149 ± 0.210 µm2 in the middle of the spindles, and 0.092 ± 0.146 µm2 at the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and can be calculated from the data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The average polygonal area of k-fibers was 0.092 ± 0.146 µm2 at the spindle poles.
source: We measured an average polygonal area of 0.034 ± 0.019 µm2 at the kinetochores, 0.149 ± 0.210 µm2 in the middle of the spindles, and 0.092 ± 0.146 µm2 at the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and can be calculated from the data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The average polygonal area of the k-fibers was about fourfold higher in the middle of the spindles compared to the position at the kinetochore.
source: Compared to the position at the kinetochore, the average polygonal area of the k-fibers was about fourfold higher in the middle of the spindles and roughly threefold higher at the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and calculated from the polygonal area measurements (0.149 µm2 / 0.034 µm2 ≈ 4.4).

claim: The average polygonal area of the k-fibers was roughly threefold higher at the spindle poles compared to the kinetochores.
source: Compared to the position at the kinetochore, the average polygonal area of the k-fibers was about fourfold higher in the middle of the spindles and roughly threefold higher at the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and calculated from the polygonal area measurements (0.092 µm2 / 0.034 µm2 ≈ 2.7).

claim: At the spindle poles, roughly only 64% of the KMTs were enclosed in the defined k-fiber circle.
source: As defined, the highest percentage of enclosed KMTs was observed at the outer kinetochore. However, at the spindle poles, roughly only 64% of the KMTs were enclosed (Table 4).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Table 4.

claim: The density of KMTs in the k-fibers at the spindle poles was decreased compared to the one observed at the outer kinetochore.
source: Thus, the density of KMTs in the k-fibers at the spindle poles was decreased compared to the one observed at the outer kinetochore (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: K-fibers display a higher tortuosity and a lower KMT density close to the spindle poles compared to the kinetochore positions, thus leading to a broadened appearance of their pole-proximal ends.
source: From all these analyses, we concluded that k-fibers display a higher tortuosity and a lower KMT density close to the spindle poles compared to the kinetochore positions, thus leading to a broadened appearance of their pole-proximal ends.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and is a synthesis of multiple measurements including tortuosity (Figure 6I), KMT density (Figure 7D), and polygonal area (Figure 7B).

claim: Only 32.6 ± 5.5% of all KMT minus ends were associated with other MTs at an interaction distance of 35 nm.
source: Considering 35 nm as an example of a possible interaction distance between two MTs connected by a single dynein motor (Amos, 1989), we observed that only 32.6 ± 5.5% of all KMT minus ends were associated with other MTs (for a visualization of the pattern of association see Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2; Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and Tables 6 and 7.

claim: Of all KMT minus ends not associated with the spindle poles, only 32.8 ± 24.9% showed an association with other MT lattices at a given distance of 35 nm.
source: Moreover, all KMT minus ends that were not associated with the spindle poles (i.e. those positioned farther than 1.7 µm away from the centrioles) only 32.8 ± 24.9% showed an association with other MT lattices at a given distance of 35 nm (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: For an interaction distance of 35 nm, roughly only 30% of the KMT minus ends in k-fibers were associated with the MT network.
source: This suggested that for an interaction distance of 35 nm roughly only 30% of the KMT minus ends in k-fibers were associated with the MT network.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and inferred from the data showing 32.6% and 32.8% association rates.

claim: For a given association distance of 35 nm, 60.7 ± 9.4% of the total number of KMT minus-end associations with MT lattices were observed at the spindle poles.
source: As an example, for a given association distance of 35 nm, 60.7 ± 9.4% of the total number of associations were observed at the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: For the chosen distance of 35 nm, 44.7 ± 5.2% of KMT minus-end associations with non-KMT lattices were observed at the spindle poles.
source: For the chosen distance of 35 nm, 44.7 ± 5.2% of these associations were observed at the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The spindle poles appeared as the major sites for interaction of KMT minus ends with neighboring MT lattices.
source: Thus, the spindle poles appeared as the major sites for interaction of KMT minus ends with neighboring MT lattices.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and inferred from the data showing preferential localization of KMT minus-end associations at spindle poles (Figure 8A-B).

claim: At 35 nm or closer to the KMT lattice, on average 42 ± 8% of KMTs were associated with either KMT or non-KMT minus ends.
source: At 35 nm or closer to the KMT lattice, we observed that on average 42 ± 8% of KMTs were associated with either KMT or non-KMT minus ends, with the majority of associations with non-KMT minus ends (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C-D; Table 8 and Table 9).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3C-D and Tables 8 and 9.

claim: More than half of the KMT lattices (59.8 ± 6.7%) associated with other MT minus ends were preferentially found at spindle poles.
source: Again, more than half of the KMT lattices (59.8 ± 6.7%) associated with other MT minus ends were preferentially found at spindle poles (Figure 8C; Figure 8—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Only 39.1 ± 4.6% of non-KMTs associated with other MT minus ends were found at the poles.
source: In contrast, only 39.1 ± 4.6% of non-KMTs associated with other MT minus ends were found at the poles (Figure 8D; Figure 8—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 3F.

claim: The interaction of KMTs with other MTs preferentially takes place at the spindle poles regardless of the association distance.
source: Again, this analysis indicated that the interaction of KMTs with other MTs preferentially takes place at the spindle poles regardless of the association distance.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and inferred from the data showing preferential localization of KMT-MT interactions at spindle poles across different association distances.

claim: A peak of association between the KMT lattices and the non-KMT minus ends was observed at a relative position of around 0.3.
source: Notably, we could observe a peak of association between the KMT lattices and the non-KMT minus ends at a relative position of around 0.3 (Figure 8D), suggesting that the KMT lattices at this position are important for interactions with non-KMTs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: For 35 nm, each non-KMT associates on average with 7.4 ± 3.1 (mean ±STD, n=16256) other MTs in the spindle with an average association length of 103±118 nm (mean ±STD, n=16256).
source: For 35 nm, each non-KMT associates on average with 7.4 ± 3.1 (mean ±STD, n=16256) other MTs in the spindle with an average association length of 103±118 nm (mean ±STD, n=16256).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by data shown in Tables 10 and 11.

claim: With an increase in the distance between MTs, KMTs tend to show a higher number and a higher average length of associations compared to non-KMTs.
source: With an increase in the distance between MTs, we observed that KMTs tend to show a higher number and a higher average length of associations compared to non-KMTs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Tables 10 and 11 and Figure 9—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: The 3D reconstructions show a distribution of KMT length in metaphase that is strikingly similar to the distribution plot of KMT length as obtained by biophysical modeling in combination with light microscopy.
source: Essentially, our 3D reconstructions show a distribution of KMT length in metaphase that is strikingly similar to the distribution plot of KMT length as obtained by biophysical modeling in combination with light microscopy (see Figure 8B-D in Conway et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by comparison with data from a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022).

claim: KMTs are on average twice as long as non-KMT.
source: Comparing the average length of KMTs and non-KMTs, we also find that KMTs are on average twice as long as non-KMT.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and can be calculated from the data showing KMT average length of 3.87 µm and non-KMT average length of 2.0 µm.

claim: A higher value in the average length of KMTs versus non-KMTs contributes to a higher percentage in the tubulin mass of KMTs compared to all other MTs in the spindle.
source: Thus, a higher value in the average length of KMTs versus non-KMTs contributes to a higher percentage in the tubulin mass of KMTs compared to all other MTs in the spindle.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the length distribution data showing KMTs are longer on average than non-KMTs.

claim: The length distribution of KMTs in HeLa cells shows striking similarities to the distribution of KMTs observed in the early C. elegans embryo.
source: The length distribution of KMTs in HeLa cells shows striking similarities to the distribution of KMTs observed in the early C. elegans embryo (Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by comparison with data from a previous study (Redemann et al., 2017).

claim: Both human KMTs attached to monocentric kinetochores and nematode KMTs associated with dispersed holocentric kinetochores show a rather flat length distribution and a rather low number of both very short and very long KMTs.
source: Both human KMTs attached to monocentric kinetochores and also nematode KMTs associated with dispersed holocentric kinetochores show a rather flat length distribution and a rather low number of both very short and very long KMTs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by comparison of the current data with previous work on C. elegans (Redemann et al., 2017).

claim: Non-KMTs in both HeLa and C. elegans systems show an exponential length distribution with a very high occurrence of very short MTs.
source: In contrast, non-KMTs in both systems show an exponential length distribution with a very high occurrence of very short MTs (around 57% of the non-KMTs and ~21% of KMT in HeLa cells were less than 2 µm in length).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the length distribution data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Exponential length distributions as found for non-KMTs are typical of dynamic instability kinetics.
source: Exponential length distributions as found for non-KMTs are typical of dynamic instability kinetics (Burbank et al., 2007; Loiodice et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies (Burbank et al., 2007; Loiodice et al., 2019).

claim: The observed length distribution of KMTs indicates a difference in dynamics and possibly higher stability of the plus-ends against MT depolymerization.
source: The observed length distribution of KMTs, however, indicates a difference in dynamics and possibly higher stability of the plus-ends against MT depolymerization.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the comparison of KMT and non-KMT length distributions.

claim: KMTs in both spindles have distinct properties different from those of non-KMTs.
source: Taken together, all this argues that KMTs in both spindles have distinct properties different from those of non-KMTs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the differences in length distributions and other properties between KMTs and non-KMTs.

claim: Cold-treated cells show cold-stable k-fibers, while most of the non-KMTs undergo depolymerization upon exposure to cold.
source: Such treated cells show cold-stable k-fibers, while most of the non-KMTs undergo depolymerization upon exposure to cold (Maiato et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous work (Maiato et al., 2004).

claim: KMTs are likely stabilized by interaction with the kinetochores.
source: Likely, KMTs are stabilized by interaction with the kinetochores (Brinkley and Cartwright, 1975; DeLuca et al., 2006; Warren et al., 2020) and/or by KMT-KMT/KMT-non-KMT associations, possibly mediated by several MT-associated proteins (Agarwal, 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies (Brinkley and Cartwright, 1975; DeLuca et al., 2006; Warren et al., 2020; Agarwal, 2018).

claim: The number of attached KMTs could be related to kinetochore size.
source: This difference in the number of attached KMTs could be related to kinetochore size.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is speculative, based on the observation that kinetochores in HeLa cells are smaller than in PtK1 cells.

claim: Kinetochores in HeLa cells are about half the size of kinetochores in PtK1 cells.
source: As previously observed by light microscopy, kinetochores in HeLa cells are about half the size of kinetochores in PtK1 cells (Cherry et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous work (Cherry et al., 1989).

claim: Kinetochore size in PtK1 cells was 0.157 ± 0.045 µm2 (mean ±STD) as observed by electron tomography.
source: Similarly, kinetochore size in PtK1 cells was 0.157 ± 0.045 µm2 (mean ±STD) as observed by electron tomography (McEwen et al., 1998a), whereas kinetochores in HeLa cells, as determined indirectly in this study, have an estimated size of about 0.107 ± 0.075 µm2 (mean ±STD).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous work (McEwen et al., 1998a).

claim: Kinetochores in HeLa cells have an estimated size of about 0.107 ± 0.075 µm2 (mean ±STD).
source: Similarly, kinetochore size in PtK1 cells was 0.157 ± 0.045 µm2 (mean ±STD) as observed by electron tomography (McEwen et al., 1998a), whereas kinetochores in HeLa cells, as determined indirectly in this study, have an estimated size of about 0.107 ± 0.075 µm2 (mean ±STD).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is based on indirect measurements from the current study.

claim: The area of the outer kinetochore might indirectly define the size and/or the number of available free binding sites for MTs.
source: Possibly, the area of the outer kinetochore might indirectly define the size and/or the number of available free binding sites for MTs (Drpic et al., 2018; Monda and Cheeseman, 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is speculative, supported by citations to previous studies (Drpic et al., 2018; Monda and Cheeseman, 2018).

claim: The number of KMTs per k-fiber is not related to the position of these KMTs in the spindles.
source: Concerning the number of kinetochore-attached MTs, it is interesting to note here that the number of KMTs per k-fiber is not related to the position of these KMTs in the spindles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3N and Table 5.

claim: Central, intermediate and peripheral kinetochores show similar average numbers of attached KMTs.
source: In fact, central, intermediate and peripheral kinetochores show similar average numbers of attached KMTs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3N and Table 5.

claim: The peripheral position of k-fibers within the spindle accompanied by an increase in the global tortuosity has no effect on the number of KMTs in the k-fibers.
source: Thus, the peripheral position of k-fibers within the spindle accompanied by an increase in the global tortuosity has no effect on the number of KMTs in the k-fibers.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the data showing no difference in KMT number across different k-fiber positions despite differences in tortuosity.

claim: KMTs in the reconstructed k-fibers are of different lengths, confirming previous observations.
source: KMTs in our reconstructed k-fibers are of different lengths, confirming previous observations (McDonald et al., 1992; O'Toole et al., 2020; Sikirzhytski et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the current data (Figure 4A) and citations to previous studies (McDonald et al., 1992; O'Toole et al., 2020; Sikirzhytski et al., 2014).

claim: Many KMTs are relatively short (~20% of KMTs were shorter than 2 µm).
source: In fact, many KMTs are relatively short (~20% of KMTs were shorter than 2 µm; Figure 4A), and half of the KMT minus ends are not positioned in the defined MT-centrosome interaction area.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Half of the KMT minus ends are not positioned in the defined MT-centrosome interaction area.
source: In fact, many KMTs are relatively short (~20% of KMTs were shorter than 2 µm; Figure 4A), and half of the KMT minus ends are not positioned in the defined MT-centrosome interaction area.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Short KMTs in k-fibers are not directly associated with the spindle poles.
source: Per definition, these short KMTs in k-fibers are not directly associated with the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the definition of the MT-centrosome interaction area and the length distribution of KMTs.

claim: Only 5% of the analyzed k-fibers show a length distribution in which none of the analyzed KMTs is positioned in the MT-centrosome interaction area.
source: Interestingly, only 5% of the analyzed k-fibers show a length distribution in which none of the analyzed KMTs is positioned in the MT-centrosome interaction area (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the one-cell C. elegans embryo, only about 20% of the KMT minus ends were located within 2 µm of their corresponding mother centriole.
source: When analyzing KMTs in the one-cell C. elegans embryo, we found that only about 20% of the KMT minus ends were located within 2 µm of their corresponding mother centriole.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: The majority of KMTs in C. elegans do not contact the centrosomes.
source: This suggested that the majority of KMTs in C. elegans do not contact the centrosomes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the observation that only 20% of KMT minus ends were near the centrosomes in C. elegans.

claim: The k-fibers in HeLa cells mediate a semi-direct connection with the spindle poles, in which at least one KMT of the k-fibers is directly connected to the poles, while the other KMTs of the fiber are indirectly linked to non-KMTs.
source: In agreement with previously published data (McDonald et al., 1992; O'Toole et al., 2020), our tomographic analysis of mammalian KMTs thus suggests that the k-fibers in HeLa cells mediate a semi-direct connection with the spindle poles, in which at least one KMT of the k-fibers is directly connected to the poles, while the other KMTs of the fiber are indirectly linked to non-KMTs (Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the current data and citations to previous studies (McDonald et al., 1992; O'Toole et al., 2020).

claim: Spindles in nematode embryos and in mammalian cells are similar in that anchoring of KMTs into the spindle network can be observed.
source: Thus, spindles in nematode embryos and in mammalian cells are similar in that anchoring of KMTs into the spindle network can be observed.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from comparison of the current data with previous work on C. elegans.

claim: Centrally located KMTs were shorter, and their minus ends showed a shorter distance to the mother centriole compared to peripheral KMTs.
source: Centrally located KMTs were shorter, and their minus ends showed a shorter distance to the mother centriole compared to peripheral KMTs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 and Table 5.

claim: The difference in KMT length and minus-end distance between central and peripheral KMTs is most likely related to the roundedness of the mitotic spindles.
source: This difference is most likely related to the roundedness of the mitotic spindles (Taubenberger et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is speculative, supported by citation to previous work (Taubenberger et al., 2020).

claim: An increase in the tortuosity of KMTs at spindle poles might promote the anchoring of the broadened k-fibers into the non-KMT network through MT-MT interactions.
source: An increase in the tortuosity of KMTs at spindle poles might promote the anchoring of the broadened k-fibers into the non-KMT network through MT-MT interactions (Figure 10C–D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is speculative, based on the observed increase in tortuosity at spindle poles.

claim: The results obtained from the approach do not exclude models of KMT organization, in which the k-fiber is a tight bundle that continues to the pole with changing composition of KMTs and associated non-KMTs along its length.
source: Explicitly, the results obtained from our approach do not exclude models of KMT organization, in which the k-fiber is a tight bundle that continues to the pole with changing composition of KMTs and associated non-KMTs along its length.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and represents an acknowledgment of alternative interpretations of the data.

claim: Differences in either the length of KMTs or in the loss of KMTs from the k-fiber might simply reflect a MT exchange with the spindle.
source: In this sense, differences in either the length of KMTs or in the loss of KMTs from the k-fiber might simply reflect a MT exchange with the spindle (Figure 10D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is speculative, representing an alternative interpretation of the data.

claim: The consideration of KMTs as the cores of k-fibers is not in disagreement with a dynamic change in k-fiber composition during the maturing of those fibers in metaphase.
source: Our consideration of KMTs as the cores of k-fibers is also not in disagreement with a dynamic change in k-fiber composition during the maturing of those fibers in metaphase (Begley et al., 2021; Maiato et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies (Begley et al., 2021; Maiato et al., 2004).

claim: Both KMTs and non-KMTs show a clear correlation in the number and the average length of associations.
source: While both KMTs and non-KMTs show a clear correlation in the number and the average length of associations (Figure 9—figure supplement 2), both MT populations show differences in the position of these associations.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: KMTs show a high tendency to associate with non-KMTs at the spindle poles.
source: In contrast to non-KMTs, KMTs show a high tendency to associate with non-KMTs at the spindle poles (Figure 8F–G; Figure 9C–D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figures 8F-G and 9C-D.

claim: The tendency of KMTs to interact at spindle poles is independent of the chosen distance of MT interaction.
source: This tendency to interact at spindle poles is independent of the chosen distance of MT interaction.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the data showing preferential pole localization across different interaction distances.

claim: KMTs preferably associate with other MTs at the spindle poles.
source: In accord with the previously discussed broadening of the k-fibers at their pole-facing end, our results suggest that KMTs preferably associate with other MTs at the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data showing preferential localization of KMT-MT associations at spindle poles.

claim: Non-KMTs show a flat pattern of interaction with other MTs at association distances of 25 and 35 nm.
source: In contrast, non-KMTs show a flat pattern of interaction with other MTs at association distances of 25 and 35 nm.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: An increase in the association distance from 35 nm to 50 nm shows a higher tendency of non-KMTs to associate with MTs in the center of the spindle, very likely related to the organization of interpolar MTs in the center of the spindle.
source: Moreover, an increase in the association distance from 35 nm to 50 nm, shows a higher tendency of non-KMTs to associate with MTs in the center of the spindle, very likely related to the organization of interpolar MTs in the center of the spindle (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F; Kajtez et al., 2016; Mastronarde et al., 1993; Vukušić et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1F and citations to previous studies (Kajtez et al., 2016; Mastronarde et al., 1993; Vukušić et al., 2017).

claim: A model was proposed in which KMTs predominantly nucleate de novo at kinetochores, with KMTs growing towards the spindle poles.
source: Combining data on the length and the position of KMT minus ends in spindles (as obtained here by electron microscopy), and the turnover and movement of tubulin in KMTs as generated by light microscopy, a model was proposed in which KMTs predominantly nucleate de novo at kinetochores, with KMTs growing towards the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and refers to a model proposed in a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022).

claim: KMTs in spindles grow along the same trajectories as non-KMTs and both the KMTs and non-KMTs are well aligned throughout the spindle.
source: A major outcome of this parallel study is that KMTs in spindles grow along the same trajectories as non-KMTs and that both the KMTs and non-KMTs are well aligned throughout the spindle, leading to the assumption that spindles can be considered as active liquid crystals (Brugués and Needleman, 2014; Oriola et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and refers to findings from a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022) with additional citations (Brugués and Needleman, 2014; Oriola et al., 2020).

claim: Spindles can be considered as active liquid crystals.
source: A major outcome of this parallel study is that KMTs in spindles grow along the same trajectories as non-KMTs and that both the KMTs and non-KMTs are well aligned throughout the spindle, leading to the assumption that spindles can be considered as active liquid crystals (Brugués and Needleman, 2014; Oriola et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies (Brugués and Needleman, 2014; Oriola et al., 2020) and findings from a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022).

claim: The analyzed spindles show a high nematic order parameter (S = 0.81 ± 0.02) near the chromosomes.
source: Interestingly, the analyzed spindles show a high nematic order parameter (S = 0.81 ± 0.02) near the chromosomes, whereas the nematic order parameter (S = 0.54 ± 0.02) is lower at the spindle poles (Conway et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and refers to data from a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022).

claim: The nematic order parameter (S = 0.54 ± 0.02) is lower at the spindle poles.
source: Interestingly, the analyzed spindles show a high nematic order parameter (S = 0.81 ± 0.02) near the chromosomes, whereas the nematic order parameter (S = 0.54 ± 0.02) is lower at the spindle poles (Conway et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and refers to data from a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022).

claim: KMTs are well aligned in the middle of the spindle, while the order of the KMTs in the k-fibers is progressively lost at positions closer to the spindle poles.
source: Along this line, KMTs in our electron tomography study are well aligned in the middle of the spindle, while the order of the KMTs in the k-fibers is progressively lost at positions closer to the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the tortuosity analysis shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The observed broadening of the k-fibers at the spindle poles might be a direct consequence of a decrease in the internal structural organization of the spindle trajectories.
source: While KMTs are growing out from the kinetochores towards the centrosomes, the observed broadening of the k-fibers at the spindle poles might be a direct consequence of a decrease in the internal structural organization of the spindle trajectories (i.e. of the surrounding non-KMTs).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is speculative, based on the observed broadening and the concept of spindles as liquid crystals.

claim: The use of plastic sections suffers from the fact that samples undergo a collapse in the electron beam during imaging, which is obvious by a reduction in the section thickness.
source: The use of plastic sections suffers from the fact that samples undergo a collapse in the electron beam during imaging, and this is obvious by a reduction in the section thickness (Luther et al., 1988; McEwen and Marko, 1998; O'Toole et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous studies (Luther et al., 1988; McEwen and Marko, 1998; O'Toole et al., 2020).

claim: By expanding the complete stack of serial tomograms, it is possible to correct the loss in Z due to sample collapse.
source: By expanding the complete stack of serial tomograms (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), it is possible to correct this loss in Z, and we did so for our three data sets covering whole metaphase spindles in HeLa cells.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The 3D reconstructions show a distribution of KMT length in metaphase that is strikingly similar to the distribution plot of KMT length as obtained by biophysical modeling in combination with light microscopy.
source: Essentially, our 3D reconstructions show a distribution of KMT length in metaphase that is strikingly similar to the distribution plot of KMT length as obtained by biophysical modeling in combination with light microscopy (see Figure 8B-D in Conway et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by comparison with data from a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022).

claim: Light and electron microscopy produces truly complementary data, although completely different methods of sample preparation and data analysis have to be applied.
source: All this shows that light and electron microscopy produces truly complementary data, although completely different methods of sample preparation and data analysis have to be applied.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the comparison of EM and light microscopy data.
